docs.title: BlackBox Flight Recorder
docs.description: Event recording and post-mortem debugging for HORUS applications
docs.content: BlackBox Flight Recorder The BlackBox flight recorder provides continuous event logging for post-mortem analysis. Like an aircraft flight recorder, it captures all significant events leading up to failures in a circular buffer. Overview The BlackBox: - Records scheduler, node, and safety events automatically - Uses a fixed-size circular buffer (oldest events discarded when full) - Captures anomalies (errors, deadline misses, emergency stops) - Requires no manual instrumentation — the Scheduler records events automatically Enabling BlackBox Use a Scheduler preset that includes the BlackBox: What Gets Recorded The BlackBox automatically captures events during scheduler execution: Description When the scheduler begins and ends Node execution Failed node executions Deadline misses Nodes that exceeded their execution time budget Circuit breaker changes Safety system activations Custom events Post-Mortem Debugging After a failure, the BlackBox contains the sequence of events leading up to it. Use the Scheduler's blackbox access to inspect: Circular Buffer Behavior The BlackBox uses a fixed-size circular buffer. When full, the oldest events are discarded: This ensures bounded memory usage while keeping the most recent events for debugging. Recommended Buffer Sizes Preset deploy() hardrealtime() safetycritical() See Also - Safety Monitor - Real-time safety monitoring - Circuit Breaker - Fault tolerance patterns - Record & Replay - Full recording and playback

docs.title: Circuit Breaker
docs.description: Fault tolerance pattern for preventing cascading failures in node execution
docs.content: Circuit Breaker The circuit breaker pattern prevents cascading failures by temporarily disabling failing nodes. When a node fails repeatedly, the circuit "opens" to stop calling it, giving it time to recover. Overview Circuit breakers protect against: - Cascading failures from one failing node - Resource exhaustion from repeated retry attempts - System-wide slowdowns from blocked calls The Scheduler manages circuit breakers automatically — you enable them via a preset and the scheduler handles state transitions, timeouts, and recovery. States Description Normal operation Too many failures Testing recovery <MermaidDiagram chart={%%{init: {'flowchart': {'padding': 20}}}%% stateDiagram-v2 [] --Closed Closed --Open : failure threshold Open --HalfOpen : timeout HalfOpen --Closed : success threshold HalfOpen --Open : failure } caption="Circuit breaker state transitions" /How It Works Closed → Open When a node's failures reach the threshold, the circuit opens and the node is temporarily disabled: Open → Half-Open After the timeout elapses, the scheduler allows a single trial execution: Half-Open → Closed If the trial succeeds enough times, the circuit closes and the node resumes normal operation: Enabling Circuit Breakers Use a Scheduler preset that includes circuit breakers: Per-Node Failure Policies Configure different failure handling per node using the node builder: Failure policies: Behavior Stop the scheduler immediately FailurePolicy::Restart { maxrestarts, delayms } Log the failure, continue running | When circuit breakers are enabled, nodes use their tier's default failure policy unless overridden. Monitoring Circuit breaker state changes are automatically recorded in the BlackBox flight recorder. After a failure, inspect the blackbox to see state transitions: Best Practices 1. Use presets: Scheduler::deploy() or Scheduler::highperformance() enable circuit breakers with sensible defaults. 2. Set failure policies per node: Critical nodes should use FailurePolicy::F

docs.title: Deterministic Execution
docs.description: Achieving reproducible execution in HORUS for testing, debugging, and safety certification
docs.content: Deterministic Execution HORUS supports deterministic execution where the same inputs produce identical outputs every run. This is useful for debugging, regression testing, and safety-critical systems. Why Determinism Matters Debugging: Non-deterministic bugs are hard to reproduce. Deterministic mode lets you replay exact sequences. Testing: Repeatable unit tests and regression testing require the same outputs for the same inputs. Safety Certification: Standards like ISO 26262 and IEC 62443 require predictable execution timing and reproducible behavior. Determinism Levels HORUS offers different levels of deterministic guarantees: Config Use Case Scheduler::new() Most applications + Performance Basic + explicit optimization tiers Scheduler::safetycritical() Medical, industrial + Full Virtual time, seeded RNG, execution tracing Level 1: Basic Determinism (Default) Scheduler::new() is deterministic out of the box: Guarantees: - Sequential execution (same order every tick) - No learning phase (no runtime profiling) - Reproducible runs with same inputs Level 2: Determinism + Performance Tiers Use .tier() to get deterministic execution with explicit performance tiers: Node tiers: Description Ultra-fast inline (<1μs) Inline execution (<10μs) Standard scheduling (<100μs+) Tiers are explicit — no runtime profiling needed, so execution is fully deterministic. Level 3: Determinism + Safety Use Scheduler::safetycritical() for safety-critical systems: Adds: - Watchdog timers (100ms timeout) - WCET enforcement - Deadline monitoring - Memory locking (mlockall) - Real-time scheduling class (SCHEDFIFO) - Safety monitor with zero tolerance for deadline misses Level 4: Full Deterministic Mode Use Scheduler::deterministic() for full reproducibility with virtual time: Adds: - Virtual time (deterministic clock instead of wall clock) - Seeded RNG (all randomness derived from seed 42) - Execution tracing via the built-in recording system - BlackBox flight recorder (100MB) - Static

docs.title: Execution Modes
docs.description: Understanding HORUS scheduler execution modes: Sequential and Parallel
docs.content: Execution Modes <Callout type="info" title="Quick Answer: Which Mode Should I Use?"Use the default. Scheduler::new() gives you deterministic, predictable execution that works for most robots. Recommended Preset Default (Scheduler::new()) Prototyping Scheduler::highperformance() Safety-critical (medical, aerospace) Don't overthink this. Pick one and change later if needed. </CalloutHORUS supports two execution modes to optimize for different robotics scenarios. You choose the mode through scheduler presets — the scheduler handles the rest. Sequential Mode The deterministic choice for safety-critical systems. Sequential mode is the default. Nodes execute one-by-one in priority order, producing the same execution order every tick. How It Works - Nodes execute one-by-one in priority order - Same execution order every tick - Bit-for-bit reproducible runs Characteristics Value 100-500ns per node Deterministic No (single thread) Best For When to Use - Medical/surgical robots requiring certification - Systems needing reproducible behavior - Debugging complex timing issues - Formal verification scenarios These presets use sequential mode: Scheduler::new(), Scheduler::safetycritical(), Scheduler::deterministic(). Parallel Mode Multi-core execution for maximum throughput. Parallel mode schedules independent nodes on different CPU cores, executing them concurrently while still respecting priority ordering. How It Works - Schedules independent nodes on different cores - Respects priority ordering - Uses thread pool for concurrent execution Characteristics Value Variable (depends on workload) Deterministic Yes Best For When to Use - Multi-sensor robots - Compute-heavy pipelines - Systems with many independent nodes - When you have multiple CPU cores available The Scheduler::highperformance() and Scheduler::hardrealtime() presets use parallel mode: Mode Comparison Sequential Yes No 87-313ns Yes Examples Safety-Critical System Racing Robot Multi-Sensor Robot Next Steps - Learn abou

docs.title: Network Backends
docs.description: Communication backends in HORUS — automatic local IPC with planned network transport
docs.content: Communication Backends HORUS automatically selects the optimal communication backend based on topology — no configuration needed. All current backends are local (same-machine), using shared memory or in-process channels. <Callout type="warn" title="Network Transport Not Yet Available"HORUS currently operates as a local shared memory IPC framework only. Network transport (Zenoh, UDP, etc.) is planned but no network backend code exists yet. All topics created with Topic::new("name") use local shared memory or in-process channels. This page documents the existing backends and the planned network direction. </CalloutAutomatic Backend Selection When you call Topic::new("name"), HORUS automatically detects the optimal backend based on the number of publishers, subscribers, and whether they're in the same process: No configuration needed. The backend upgrades and downgrades dynamically as participants join and leave. docs.title: Safety Monitor
docs.description: Real-time safety monitoring with watchdogs, WCET enforcement, and emergency stop
docs.content: Safety Monitor The Safety Monitor provides real-time safety monitoring for safety-critical robotics applications. It enforces timing constraints, monitors node health, and triggers emergency stops when safety violations occur. Overview The Safety Monitor includes: - Watchdogs: Monitor node liveness — trigger emergency stop if a critical node hangs - WCET Enforcement: Worst-Case Execution Time budgets — halt if a node takes too long - Deadline Tracking: Count deadline misses and trigger emergency stop at threshold - Emergency Stop: Immediate system halt on critical failures The Scheduler manages the safety monitor internally — you enable it via a preset and the scheduler automatically feeds watchdogs, checks WCET, and triggers emergency stops. Enabling Safety Monitoring Use a Scheduler preset that includes safety monitoring: What Each Preset Enables safetycritical() Yes Yes Yes (100ms) 0 (zero tolerance) Yes Yes Configuring Critical Nodes After choosing a preset, register critical nodes with timing constraints using the node builder: Watchdogs Watchdogs monitor node liveness. The scheduler automatically feeds watchdogs on successful node ticks. If a critical node fails to execute within the watchdog timeout, an emergency stop is triggered. Timeout Guidelines WCET Enforcement Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) budgets ensure nodes complete within time limits. Set budgets via the node builder: For critical nodes, WCET violations trigger an emergency stop. For non-critical nodes, violations are logged and recorded in the BlackBox. Emergency Stop Emergency stop is triggered automatically by: - Critical node watchdog expiration - Critical node WCET violation - Critical node deadline miss - Exceeding the maxdeadlinemisses threshold When emergency stop triggers: 1. All node execution is halted 2. An emergency stop event is recorded in the BlackBox 3. The scheduler transitions to emergency state Inspecting After Emergency Stop Best Practices 1. Start with Conservative Budgets

docs.title: Communication Patterns Overview
docs.description: Understanding HORUS communication primitives — Topics, Actions, and Network
docs.content: Communication Patterns Overview HORUS provides two communication primitives that cover all robotics messaging needs: Purpose Streaming data (pub/sub) Long-running tasks (goal/feedback/result) Both work locally (shared memory) and across machines (network transport via configuration). Topic: Streaming Pub/Sub Topic<Tis the primary communication primitive. It provides lock-free, zero-copy pub/sub with automatic backend selection from 10 optimized paths. Automatic Backend Selection You never choose a backend — HORUS detects the optimal one automatically based on: - Topology: Same thread, same process, or cross-process - Participants: How many publishers and subscribers - Type: Whether the message type is POD (Plain Old Data) Latency 3ns 18ns 24ns 26ns 36ns 50ns 65ns 70ns 85ns 167ns The backend can change at runtime — if a second subscriber joins a 1P1C topic, HORUS automatically migrates from SPSC to SPMC without dropping messages. Key Characteristics - Infallible send: send() always succeeds. Ring buffer overwrites oldest message when full ("keep last" semantics). - Non-blocking recv: recv() returns Option<T. Returns None if no message available. - Zero introspection overhead: No timing, logging, or tracing in the default path. Opt-in via withlogging(). For full Topic API details, see Topic Communication. Action: Long-Running Tasks Actions handle tasks that take time to complete and benefit from progress feedback and cancellation. They follow the Goal / Feedback / Result pattern. docs.title: Core Concepts - POD Types
docs.description: How HORUS auto-detects POD types for zero-serialization, ultra-fast communication
docs.content: POD Types and Zero-Serialization When you use Topic<T, HORUS automatically detects whether your message type is POD (Plain Old Data). POD types bypass serialization entirely — messages are transferred as raw bytes via direct memory copy, achieving 50ns latency instead of 167ns with bincode serialization. You don't need a separate API. The same Topic::new() call automatically selects the fastest path for your type. How Auto-Detection Works At topic creation time, HORUS checks: - No destructor — The type has no Drop impl (no heap pointers like String, Vec, Box) - Non-zero size — Not a zero-sized type If both are true, HORUS uses the zero-copy memcpy path. If not, it falls back to bincode serialization. This happens transparently — you always use the same Topic<TAPI: Performance Impact POD detection affects which cross-process backend is selected: POD Required Use Case Yes Broadcast to multiple consumers MpscShm 65ns Yes One producer, many consumers SpscShm 85ns No Many-to-many (non-POD fallback) Message CmdVel 2D position and orientation Twist 3D transformation with timestamp Point3 3D vector Quaternion Sensors Description Inertial measurement unit data LaserScan Position/velocity estimate Range Battery level and status NavSatFix Control Description Individual motor control DifferentialDriveCommand Servo position/velocity JointCommand PWM signal output StepperCommand Trajectory waypoint PidConfig Diagnostics Description Liveness signal NodeHeartbeat General status report EmergencyStop Safety system state ResourceUsage Single diagnostic measurement DiagnosticReport Navigation Description Navigation goal GoalResult Navigation waypoint Path Planned path VelocityObstacle Set of velocity obstacles Message WrenchStamped Force control command TactileArray Impedance control config ContactInfo Haptic output command Message JoystickInput Keyboard key events Message HorusTensor Custom POD Messages To make your own types use the fast path, implement the PodMessage trait: Requirem

It manages the node lifecycle, coordinates priority-based execution, and handles graceful shutdown. What is the Scheduler? docs.title: Core Concepts - Shared Memory
docs.description: How HORUS uses shared memory for cross-process communication
docs.content: Shared Memory When nodes run in different processes, HORUS automatically uses shared memory for communication. You don't need to configure anything — Topic::new() detects the topology and switches to shared memory backends transparently. When Shared Memory is Used HORUS auto-selects the communication backend based on where publishers and subscribers are: Backend DirectChannel (3ns) SpscIntra/MpmcIntra (18-36ns) PodShm/SpscShm/MpmcShm (50-167ns) You always use the same API: When a second process opens the same topic name, HORUS automatically migrates to a shared memory backend. Cross-Process Communication HORUS uses a flat namespace — all processes on the same machine share the same topic space. No configuration needed: Both processes automatically communicate through the shared memory file. This is similar to how ROS topics work. Topic Isolation If you need to run multiple independent HORUS applications on the same machine, use topic name prefixes: These create separate shared memory files and don't interfere with each other. Storage Locations HORUS stores shared memory in platform-specific directories: Path /dev/shm/horus/ /tmp/horus/ %TEMP%\horus\ Directory Structure Separate from the main directory: File Naming Each topic creates a file named horus{topicname}: Capacity and Memory Usage Auto-Sizing By default, Topic::new() automatically calculates capacity based on the message type size: - Small types like f32 (4 bytes): 1024 slots - Medium types like CmdVel (16 bytes): 256 slots - Larger types: Minimum 16 slots Custom Capacity Use Topic::withcapacity() for explicit control: Memory Per Topic Each topic's shared memory file contains: HEADER (640B) + SEQARRAY (capacity × 8B) + DATA (capacity × slotsize). Small POD types (≤56 bytes) use a co-located 64-byte slot layout. Larger types use DEFAULTSLOTSIZE (8 KB). docs.description: What HORUS is trying to achieve and the problems it solves
docs.content: Goals & Vision What is HORUS Trying to Achieve? HORUS aims to become the de facto standard for real-time robotics communication by providing an ultra-low latency, memory-safe, and developer-friendly framework that bridges the gap between research prototyping and production deployment. Core Objectives Sub-Microsecond Communication: Achieve 85ns-500ns latency for robotics messages, enabling real-time control loops at 1kHz+ frequencies Zero Compromise Performance: Deliver 100-270x faster performance than traditional frameworks without sacrificing safety or ease of use Memory Safety by Default: Leverage Rust's type system to eliminate entire classes of bugs common in C++ robotics frameworks Unified High-Level Workflow: Single command for build, run, and deployment across Rust and Python with minimal configuration (simple horus.yaml vs complex ROS XML) Dependency Isolation: Solve dependency hell with portable, isolated environments and reproducible builds Developer Experience First: From prototype to production without friction - auto-detect, auto-install, just run Problems HORUS Solves High IPC Latency in Traditional Frameworks Problem: Traditional middleware introduces 50-500µs of latency, which is too slow for high-frequency control loops required in modern robotics. HORUS Solution: - Shared memory architecture with zero-copy semantics - 85ns (Topic SPSC) / 500ns (Topic MPMC) for CmdVel (16B messages) - 900ns (Topic SPSC) / 2.2µs (Topic MPMC) for LaserScan (1.5KB messages) - Linear scaling with message size Impact: Enables 1kHz+ control loops for precise manipulation, high-speed drones, and real-time sensor fusion. Memory Safety Issues Problem: C++ frameworks are prone to memory leaks, use-after-free, data races, and segmentation faults that cause robot crashes in production. docs.title: Message Types
docs.description: Standard HORUS message types for robotics applications
docs.content: Message Types HORUS provides a comprehensive library of standard message types for robotics. All built-in messages are designed for shared memory efficiency — most use fixed-size structures with zero-copy POD semantics. Message Requirements Any type used with Topic<Tmust satisfy these trait bounds: A minimal custom message: For zero-copy performance, make your type POD — see POD Types for details. Typed Messages vs Generic Messages Typed Messages (Recommended) Strongly-typed Rust structs — all available via use horus::prelude::: Benefits: - Ultra-fast: 50-167ns IPC latency (zero-copy shared memory for POD types) - Type safety: Compile-time checks prevent type mismatches - IDE support: Autocomplete, type hints, inline documentation - Cross-language: Rust and Python see the same typed data Generic Messages (Prototyping) Dynamic data for arbitrary structures using GenericMessage: GenericMessage uses MessagePack serialization with a 4KB maximum payload. It has an inline buffer for small messages (≤256 bytes) and an overflow buffer for larger ones. Tradeoffs: - Flexible — any data structure, evolving schemas - Slower IPC — serialization overhead vs zero-copy POD types - No compile-time type safety Use generic messages for quick prototypes, external JSON integrations, or truly dynamic schemas. Default to typed messages for production code. Performance Comparison Typed Messages 50-167ns (POD) Compile-time Full autocomplete Production LogSummary Trait The LogSummary trait provides human-readable summaries for logging. It is not required for basic Topic::new() usage, but is required if you want logging via Topic::withlogging(). When is LogSummary Used? - Topic::new("name")? — no LogSummary required, no logging overhead - Topic::new("name")?.withlogging() — requires T: LogSummary, enables logging on send/recv When logging is active, logsummary() is called once per send/recv. Logs appear in the console, in the shared memory ring buffer at /dev/shm/horuslogs, and in horus monit

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.description: Avoid these common beginner pitfalls when using HORUS
docs.content: Common Mistakes New to HORUS? Here are the most common mistakes beginners make and how to fix them. 1. Using Slashes in Topic Names The Problem: Error: No such file or directory Why: HORUS uses shared memory files in /dev/shm/. Slashes in topic names are interpreted as directory paths. The Fix: 2. Forgetting to Call recv() Every Tick The Problem: Why: Messages can be missed if you don't check every tick. Topic uses a ring buffer (16-1024 slots by default), and old messages are overwritten when the buffer fills up. The Fix: 3. Blocking in tick() The Problem: Why: All nodes run in a single tick cycle. Blocking one node blocks them all. The Fix: 4. Wrong Priority Order The Problem: Why: Lower order number = runs first. Safety-critical code should be order 0. The Fix: 5. Not Implementing shutdown() for Motors The Problem: Why: When you press Ctrl+C, the motor keeps running at its last velocity! The Fix: 6. Not Deriving Required Traits for Custom Messages The Problem: Why: Topic requires types to implement Clone, Serialize, and Deserialize. The Fix: Or use the standard message types which already have the required traits: 7. Thinking send() Returns a Result The Problem: Why: send() returns (), not Result. It uses ring buffer "keep last" semantics — when the buffer is full, the oldest message is overwritten. This means send() always succeeds. The Fix: 8. Creating Topic Inside tick() The Problem: Why: Creating a Topic is expensive (opens shared memory). Doing it every tick wastes resources. The Fix: 9. Mismatched Topic Types The Problem: Why: HORUS doesn't check types at runtime. Mismatched types cause data corruption. The Fix: Pro tip: Use named message types to avoid confusion: 10. Using Raw Node Trait When node! Macro Would Be Simpler The Problem: The Fix: See node! Macro for more examples. docs.content: Environment Management Environment management in HORUS allows you to capture, save, and restore the exact set of packages and versions used in your project. Perfect for reproducible builds, team collaboration, and deployment. Overview Think of environments like Python's requirements.txt or Node's package-lock.json: - Freeze your current environment to a file - Restore environments on different machines - Share setups with teammates - Deploy exact versions to production robots - Track environment history in version control Understanding HORUS's Hidden Environment HORUS automatically manages a hidden .horus/ environment in each project. Understanding the global vs local architecture helps you work efficiently across multiple projects. Global Cache (Shared Storage) Location: /.horus/cache/ All packages are downloaded once and stored here: Benefits: - Download once - Use in all projects - Saves disk space - No duplication - Faster setup - Cached packages install instantly - Works offline - Already have what you need Local Workspace (Project-Specific) Location: .horus/ in your project Each project gets its own isolated environment: Key Points: - Workspace marker - .horus/ identifies a HORUS project - Symlinks not copies - Points to global cache (lightweight!) - Isolated - Each project independent - Auto-managed - Created by horus run, not by you Automatic Workflow When you run horus run: 1. docs.content: Creating CLI Plugins A CLI plugin is a standalone binary that adds a subcommand to horus. When a user runs horus mycommand, HORUS discovers your plugin binary and executes it, passing through all arguments. Zero-Config Convention Any Rust package named horus- with a [[bin]] target is automatically detected as a plugin. No extra configuration required. Example: A package named horus-sim3d with [[bin]] name = "sim3d" automatically provides the horus sim3d command. Step-by-Step Guide Step 1: Create a New Rust Project Step 2: Set Up Cargo.toml The key points: - Package name starts with horus- - The [[bin]] name defines the subcommand (users will run horus mycommand) - Use clap or similar for argument parsing Step 3: Implement the Plugin Step 4: Build and Test Locally Step 5: Install Locally To test with the actual horus CLI, install the binary where HORUS can find it: Now horus mycommand --help should work. Environment Variables HORUS sets these environment variables when executing plugins: Value 1 e.g., 0.1.7 Your plugin inherits the user's stdin, stdout, and stderr, so interactive prompts and colored output work normally. Plugin Discovery HORUS discovers plugin binaries in this order: 1. Project plugins.lock — .horus/plugins.lock in the current project 2. Global plugins.lock — /.horus/plugins.lock 3. docs.title: TensorPool API
docs.description: Zero-copy tensor memory management for high-performance robotics and AI/ML
docs.content: TensorPool API HORUS provides efficient tensor memory management through shared memory pools, enabling zero-copy data sharing between processes for both CPU and GPU tensors. Overview The TensorPool system consists of: - TensorPool - CPU tensor allocation via shared memory - CudaTensorPool - GPU tensor allocation with CUDA IPC support - TensorHandle - RAII wrapper for automatic memory management - HorusTensor - 168-byte Pod tensor descriptor (metadata only) - Device - Pod-safe device location (Device::cpu(), Device::cuda(N)) All tensor types are available via use horus::prelude::. Auto-Managed Pools (Recommended) The simplest way to use tensor pools is through Topic<HorusTensor, which auto-manages a pool per topic: The pool is created lazily on first use and shared across all Topic<HorusTensorinstances with the same name — even across processes. Pool IDs are derived deterministically from the topic name using FNV-1a hashing. Manual CPU TensorPool For advanced use cases requiring direct pool control. Priority-Based Safety System Use node priorities to ensure safety-critical tasks always run first - essential for production robotics. File: safetysystem.rs Run it: Key Concepts: - Priority 0 (Critical): Emergency stop - runs first, always - Priority 1 (High): Motor control - runs after safety checks - Priority 4 (Background): Logging - runs last, non-critical - Lower number = higher priority - Safety systems should always check estop before acting 3. docs.content: Troubleshooting Runtime Errors This guide helps you diagnose and fix common errors that occur when running HORUS applications. For installation issues, see Installation Troubleshooting. Quick Diagnostic Steps When your HORUS application isn't working: 1. Check the Monitor: Run horus monitor to see active nodes, topics, and message flow 2. Examine Logs: Look for error messages in your terminal output 3. Verify Topics: Ensure publisher and subscriber use exact same topic names 4. Check Shared Memory: Look in /dev/shm/horus/ for stale HORUS memory regions 5. Test Individually: Run nodes one at a time to isolate the problem Topic Creation Errors Error: "Topic creation failed" or "Failed to create Topic<T" Symptom: Application crashes on startup with: Common Causes: 1. Stale Shared Memory from Previous Run - HORUS uses /dev/shm/horus/ directory for communication - If your app crashes, these files persist Fix: Clean shared memory: 2. Permission Issues - You may not have write access to /dev/shm/ Fix: Check permissions: 3. Conflicting Topic Names - Two Topics with same name but different types Fix: Use unique topic names: Error: "No such file or directory" when creating Topic Symptom: Application crashes with: Cause: You're using slashes (/) in your topic name. While slashes work on Linux (parent directories are created automatically), they fail on macOS where shared memory uses shmopen() which doesn't support embedded slashes. HORUS topic names map to files under /dev/shm/horus/topics/ on Linux: Fix: Use dots instead of slashes for cross-platform compatibility: Coming from ROS? ROS uses slashes (/sensor/lidar) because it uses network-based naming. HORUS uses dots because topic names map directly to shared memory file names. See Topic Naming for details. Message Communication Issues Problem: "No messages received" - recv() always returns None Symptom: Subscriber node never receives messages even though publisher is sending. Common Causes: 1.
